publisher: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) - payroll deduction formulas / rates and income thresholds; gross input sourced from Statistics Canada National Graduates Survey
raw_extract:
CRA 2026 federal income tax rates (read from 'Current year tax rates and income brackets (2026)', canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/individuals/tax-rates-brackets/current-year.html):
'Federal rate: 2026 - Each portion of your taxable income from / up to / is taxed at: $0 / $58,523 / 14%; $58,523.01 / $117,045 / 20.5%; $117,045.01 / $181,440 / 26%; $181,440.01 / $258,482 / 29%; $258,482.01 / unlimited / 33%'
The same page states: 'Provincial or territorial income tax rates apply in addition to federal income tax rates.' and 'The rate is determined by your province or territory of residence on December 31, 2026.'

CRA 2026 British Columbia income tax rates (same page, 'British Columbia rate: 2026'): $0-$50,363 at 5.6%; $50,363.01-$100,728 at 7.7%; $100,728.01-$115,648 at 10.5%; $115,648.01-$140,430 at 12.29%; $140,430.01-$190,405 at 14.7%; $190,405.01-$265,545 at 16.8%; $265,545.01 and over at 20.5%.

CRA Payroll Deductions Formulas (T4127, 123rd edition, effective 1 July 2026), read verbatim: 'On February 17, 2026, the Government of British Columbia announced a change to the lowest personal income tax rate and the BC tax reduction. For 2026 and subsequent years, the lowest personal tax rate is increased from 5.06% to 5.60%.' ... 'In addition, for 2026 and subsequent years, the basic reduction is increased from $562 to $690. The basic reduction amount was indexed to $575 effective January 1, 2026. Since this amount was used for the first six months of the year, a prorated basic reduction amount of $805 will apply for the remaining six months.'
And from the CRA T4032-BC payroll deductions general information page: 'For 2026, the federal income thresholds, the personal amounts, and the Canada employment amount have been changed based on changes in the consumer price index. The federal indexing factor for January 1, 2026 is 2.0%.' ... 'The federal personal amounts for 2026 are: Maximum basic personal amount ($) 16,452 | Minimum basic personal amount ($) 14,829' ... 'For 2026, the British Columbia non-refundable basic personal tax credit is $13,216.' ... 'The indexing factor for 2026, is 2.2%.'

CRA CPP contribution rates, maximums and exemptions (read verbatim): '2026 | $74,600 | $3,500 | $71,100 | 5.95 | $4,230.45 | $8,460.90' where the columns are Year, Maximum annual pensionable earnings, Basic exemption amount, Maximum contributory earnings, Employee and employer contribution rate (%), Maximum annual employee and employer contribution, Maximum annual self-employed contribution.

CRA / ESDC EI 2026 (read verbatim): 'Effective January 1, 2026. For all workers. The maximum insurable earnings is $68,900 ($65,700 in 2025). For example, if an employee earns $75,000 per year, premiums must be paid only on the first $68,900. For workers outside Quebec. The employee's EI premium rate is $1.63 per $100 ($1.64 in 2025), with a maximum annual EI premium of $1,123.07 ($1.077.48 in 2025).'

GROSS INPUT, read from Statistics Canada, The Daily, Chart 1, 'Median full-time employment income of 2020 postsecondary graduates in 2023, by level of study' (https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/daily-quotidien/240322/cg-b001-eng.htm): Bachelor's, employment status or plans NOT affected by the pandemic = 70,000.

FULL ARITHMETIC SHOWN (nothing else applied):
gross = 70,000
federal tax on gross = 0.14 x 58,523 + 0.205 x (70,000 - 58,523) = 8,193.22 + 2,352.79 = 10,546.01
less federal basic personal amount credit = 0.14 x 16,452 = 2,303.28
net federal tax = 8,242.73
BC tax on gross = 0.056 x 50,363 + 0.077 x (70,000 - 50,363) = 2,820.33 + 1,512.05 = 4,332.38
less BC basic personal tax credit = 0.056 x 13,216 = 740.10
less BC basic reduction = 690.00
net BC tax = 2,902.28
CPP employee contribution = 5.95% x (70,000 - 3,500) = 3,956.75
net take-home, EXCLUDING EI = 70,000 - 8,242.73 - 2,902.28 - 3,956.75 = 54,898.24 per year = 4,574.85 per month = 1,055.74 per week
EI if NOT opted out = 1.63% x 68,900 (capped at maximum insurable earnings) = 1,123.07
net take-home, INCLUDING EI = 53,775.17 per year = 4,481.26 per month = 1,034.14 per week
total deductions excluding EI = 15,101.76 = 21.57 per cent of gross; including EI = 16,224.83 = 23.18 per cent of gross

claims.statement: DERIVED, NOT PUBLISHED AS A SINGLE FIGURE BY ANY SOURCE. Applying the CRA's published 2026 federal and British Columbia tax brackets, published 2026 federal and BC basic personal amounts and the BC basic reduction, plus the 2026 CPP employee rate, to the Statistics Canada official gross median of CAD 70,000 for a 2020 bachelor's graduate in full-time employment, gives net take-home pay of CAD 54,898.24 per year = CAD 4,574.85 per month, EXCLUDING Employment Insurance premiums.

DERIVED: same calculation but INCLUDING the 2026 EI employee premium at the published rate of $1.63 per $100 of insurable earnings, capped at the published maximum insurable earnings of $68,900, i.e. the maximum annual EI premium of $1,123.07. Net = CAD 53,775.17 per year = CAD 4,481.26 per month.
DERIVED: CAD 54,898.24 / 52 = CAD 1,055.74 per week net, excluding EI, against a CAD 1,346.15 gross weekly equivalent.

DERIVED, using the LOWER pandemic-affected graduate gross figure instead: gross CAD 60,000; federal tax = 0.14 x 58,523 + 0.205 x (60,000 - 58,523) = 8,193.22 + 302.79 = 8,496.01, less federal BPA credit 2,303.28 = 6,192.72; BC tax = 0.056 x 50,363 + 0.077 x (60,000 - 50,363) = 2,820.33 + 741.99 = 3,562.38, less BC BPA credit 740.10, less BC basic reduction 690.00 = 2,132.28; CPP = 0.0595 x 56,500 = 3,361.75; EI = 0.0163 x 60,000 = 978.00. Net EXCLUDING EI = 60,000 - 6,192.72 - 2,132.28 - 3,361.75 = 48,313.24 per year = CAD 4,026.10 per month. Net INCLUDING EI = 47,335.24 per year = CAD 3,944.60 per month. Recorded alongside, not averaged with, the CAD 70,000 gross case.

assumptions: PROVINCE CHOSEN AND DECLARED: British Columbia. This is MY choice, made because BC is the one province for which I personally read every 2026 parameter (brackets, BC basic personal amount of $13,216, and the BC basic reduction of $690) from primary CRA sources in this research pass. It is not the most populous province. If the corpus needs Ontario instead, the same method applies but the Ontario basic personal amount must be sourced from Form TD1, 2026, which I did not read.

NOT THE SOURCE'S / MINE - and DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED, which makes this net figure CONSERVATIVE (slightly LOW): (a) the CPP contribution tax credit (the base 4.95% CPP portion is creditable against federal tax) has NOT been applied; (b) the enhanced/first-additional CPP portion of 1% has NOT treated as a deduction from taxable income; (c) the Canada Employment Amount credit has NOT been applied; (d) EI has been shown both with and without rather than assumed either way; (e) no federal or provincial non-refundable credits beyond the basic personal amount and the BC basic reduction have been applied; (f) no charitable donation credit, no RRSP deduction, no student-loan interest deduction, no HST/GST/GSTB credit. Including (a), (b) and (c) would raise net take-home by roughly CAD 600-800 per year.

NOT THE SOURCE'S / MINE: no marital status, dependants, or employment-province-versus-residence-province judgement was invented. The CRA states the rate 'is determined by your province or territory of residence on December 31, 2026'; I have simply assumed residence in British Columbia.

TAX YEAR vs GROSS YEAR MISMATCH - DECLARED: the tax model is 2026 while the gross input is 2023 income. This is unavoidable and inflates the deductions relative to the gross, because 2026 brackets and CPP are higher than 2023's. A 2023-matched calculation would give a somewhat higher net. Stated rather than hidden.

PART-YEAR BC WARNING - DECLARED: the CRA states that for BC the basic reduction amount 'was indexed to $575 effective January 1, 2026' and that 'since this amount was used for the first six months of the year, a prorated basic reduction amount of $805 will apply for the remaining six months.' I used the full-year $690 figure. An employee-paid reduction in BC is subject to clawback above a provincial threshold (not read in this pass), so $690 is used as the representative full-year value.
PERIOD CONVENTION: 'per month' is annual / 12 (an average month), not a payroll-period figure. The CRA's actual PAYG tables work in weekly and fortnightly pay periods.
NOT THE SOURCE'S / MINE: no averaging of figures from two sources. There is one gross input (Statistics Canada) and one tax model (CRA); the arithmetic above is a single deterministic chain.
NOT THE SOURCE'S / MINE: no FX conversion, no PPP factor, no currency hedging assumption.
notes: CANADA HAS NO OFFICIAL PUBLISHED TAKE-HOME FIGURE. This is category-3 evidence: an official GROSS figure from the national statistical agency (Statistics Canada, and unusually it is a genuine GRADUATE-specific figure) plus a complete, public, deterministic tax and contribution model published by the tax authority (CRA 2026 federal and provincial brackets, basic personal amounts, CPP and EI rates). It is labelled DERIVED, not official. Recommended figure for Canada: CAD 4,575 per month net excluding EI, or CAD 4,481 per month including EI, for a British Columbia resident. Corroborating ratio at this level: net is about 78.4 per cent of gross. IMPORTANT WARNINGS A READER WOULD BE MISLED BY: (1) the province assumption is BC, not Ontario, and interprovincial differences at this income level run to several hundred dollars a month; (2) the figure combines a 2023 gross with 2026 tax rules, which understates net; (3) it deliberately omits the CPP contribution credit and the Canada Employment Amount, so it is conservative; (4) it excludes the federal GST/HST or GSTB input tax credit, which is a real cash benefit to many employees but is a tax-credit interaction rather than a take-home pay component. Currency CAD; tax year 2026; gross income year 2023; graduate cohort 2020.
evidence_limitations: Inherits every limitation of the Statistics Canada gross input (single 2020 cohort, full-time workers only, pandemic-affected, median not mean, national pooling of provinces and fields of study - and BC is a minority of Canadian graduates). Then adds its own: a single-province tax model, a two-tax-year gap between gross and tax rules, and a set of deliberately excluded credits. The result should be treated as a well-documented order-of-magnitude take-home for a Canadian early-career full-time graduate, not as an official Canadian statistic, and not as a precise figure for any particular graduate.
